claims.claim: "the enforceable guarantee is precise: the poisoned bytes never become model context. The side effect that produced them already happened."
claims.evidence: True in substance but it omits the mechanism, and the mechanism is not uniform across runtimes. On the hook lane the guarantee is delivered by Claude Code's documented `hookSpecificOutput.updatedToolOutput` replacement (internal/aihooks/posttooluse.go:16 PostToolReplaceField; daemon returns UpdatedOutput at internal/daemon/ai_ingress.go:777-781; the Claude adapter builds it at internal/airuntime/adapters/claudecode/normalize.go:446-450). Codex has no such primitive: internal/airuntime/adapters/codex/response.go:227-233 maps EffectReplaceOutput onto `buildLegacyBlock(...)`, whose own comment reads "PostToolUse 'block' REPLACES the tool result the model consumes with the reason and CONTINUES the turn." So on Codex a span-level redaction becomes a WHOLE-RESULT block: the model loses the entire legitimate tool output, not the poisoned span. An inline comment in the same file the redaction lives in is also stale — internal/daemon/ai_ingress.go:189-191 still says PostToolUse "CANNOT redact ... it can only TAINT the session", which the D6 output-replacement path directly above it contradicts.
claims.correctedText: **Timing is the crux.** The proxy sees a tool result only on the *next* request — it was already produced locally. `PostToolUse` fires after the tool ran; the file was already read, the URL already fetched. So the enforceable guarantee is precise: *the poisoned bytes never become model context.* The side effect that produced them already happened. The mechanism differs by runtime and the difference is visible to the developer. On Claude Code the daemon returns a schema-preserving rewritten tool_response and the shim writes it to `hookSpecificOutput.updatedToolOutput`, so only the flagged span is replaced. **Codex has no output-replacement primitive**: the same decision is expressed as a PostToolUse block, which substitutes the reason string for the entire tool result. A redacted README on Codex means the agent sees none of the file.
claims.labelChange: unlabelled -> CONDITIONAL on runtime: span-level redaction SHIPS on the Claude lane; on the Codex lane the same effect SHIPS as a whole-result replacement.

additions.text: **The fence discipline, and the hole it opens.** A finding whose span lies wholly inside a non-instruction region — a fenced code block, a block or line comment, a markdown blockquote, an inline code span, or a one-line quoted string — is marked, demoted one severity step (high to medium, medium to low) and graded weak evidence. It is never deleted, and an admin who has explicitly mapped that class to block still blocks. This exists because the detectors previously matched on presence alone, and the measured consequence was a run of refusals on engineering work *about this product*, including the adversarial review of one of its own security fixes. Four guards stop it becoming a free pass: demotion is class-wide, so one free-standing occurrence anywhere keeps the whole class at full strength; the three HIGH combinations survive fencing, demoted to medium rather than to silence; the smuggling classes (invisible characters, decode-confirmed payloads, and anything that surfaced only after Unicode normalisation) are exempt from demotion entirely; and an unbalanced delimiter creates no region at all, so opening a fence and never closing it does not free the rest of the document. The residual is recorded rather than hidden: **a single-signal injection an attacker wraps in a fence, a blockquote or a pair of double quotes is demoted from warn to allow.** This discipline applies to the developer's own prompt only. The ingress lane calls `ScanVerbatim` and is governed byte-for-byte without it, because "the author is showing me this, not telling me this" is an inference that holds for text a developer wrote and fails completely for text arriving from a tool, an MCP server or a fetched page — which is exactly where a planted payload sits, and is made of fences and quotations to begin with.

additions.text: Three failure modes of the taint store the mechanism does not advertise. **At the cap it drops new, not old**: with 1,024 tainted buckets live, a newly poisoned session is silently not tainted and its next risky tool call is not held — the cap protects the daemon's memory against a token-bearing local caller, and it does so by failing open on the newest session. **Expiry is lazy**, evaluated on read, so a bucket past 30 minutes reads clean and is pruned at that moment. And **taint is armed once per (bucket, tool result)**: the proxy re-scans the same poisoned tool_result on every subsequent request, and each re-scan used to refresh the 30-minute clock, so a single ingress held a session open-endedly. That is now fixed by an arm key that is deliberately *not* the event dedup key — the dedup key omits the session so the proxy's session-less report and the hook's real-session report of one tool result collapse into one console event, while both buckets still arm.

additions.text: "Sixteen locations" is sixteen registry entries, not sixteen files: ten of them are directory sources with several accepted basenames apiece, so the number of paths actually examined on a developer box is higher. Coverage is bounded in two other ways worth stating. A config file over 5 MiB is refused as unreadable rather than read. And project-scope sources sweep at most 64 project roots — a developer with more checkouts than that has un-swept ones, and no coverage row says so. Registration also does not imply a recursive walk: that is a separate flag, split out after a measurement found `%APPDATA%/Code/User` holds 29,948 files across 5,918 directories on a working developer machine, so adding a location must never silently add a traversal to every startup and every six-hourly sweep.

additions.text: The shim gate's budget is four seconds, and its expiry is a fall-through rather than a stop — a timeout surfaces as the transport failure and the launch proceeds. That is the deliberate cooperative posture: a daemon blip must not stop a developer launching their agent, and the managed-endpoint case is closed upstream, where a managed box with no reachable daemon is refused outright before this code is reached. The decision itself is fetched from the daemon rather than computed in the shim, so a hold arms and consumes the same allow-once record the hook lanes use — deciding locally would print a release instruction the shim could not honour.

omissions.what: §7.5 is titled "MCP servers, plugins and skills" and says nothing about skills.
omissions.whyItMatters: The skill lane is roughly 2,600 lines of shipped non-test code implementing a load-time artifact gate with a two-axis decision, and it is the lane the plugin gates are built on top of — the plugin Decision type literally embeds skillgate.Decision. omissions.proposedText: Add a **Skills.** paragraph: "A skill invocation is gated at load time on two orthogonal axes. The knowledge axis asks what anyone knows about these exact bytes — settled clean, settled with findings, settled malicious, analysis in flight, never seen, could not be resolved to an identity at all, or a class that has no content address so no verdict about its bytes can exist. The decision axis asks what the organisation has said to do about an artifact in that state. They are deliberately not collapsed: folding \"the org accepted an unknown\" into \"the scanner settled clean\" would destroy the never-seen-ness, and never-seen is the signal that gets the artifact submitted for analysis in the first place — an org that allows unscanned skills still wants its catalog populated. reorganisation:
Four changes, in order of value.

1. **Split §7.4's honest notes into "unwired" and "wired but weak", and give each item a label.** Today the section mixes six "cannot stop" bullets (three of which are structural detector limits and three of which are unwired code) with three "honest notes" (two of which are engine facts and one of which is a shipped-default consequence). A reader cannot tell which items would be fixed by an assignment and which are design. Proposed structure: **(a) Detector limits — permanent**: not English, free-form-gap line splits, indirection, side effects already performed. **(b) Built and not running — INERT, with the missing assignment named**: cross-message correlator (zero callers; the daemon owns the session store and never builds the window), streamed model output (`OutputStreamObserver` has no writer), destination annotation (`Destinations()` has no caller and the field is not on the wire), ingress force-taint (`taintClasses` is never emitted by the Backend). **(c) Running, and weaker than the console implies — CONDITIONAL**: hold is byte-identical to redact; `ingress-remote-code-exec` warns and records nothing and has no policy vocabulary; the proxy taint holds nothing on its own; the shipped default's monitor placement of `ingress-exfil-verb` disarms the `poisoned-read-exfil` taint shape. Every item in (b) should name the one line that would wire it, so the section doubles as a work list — that is the property that makes an inert inventory worth accumulating.

2. **Move the taint bar out of the rules paragraph and give it its own subsection.** It is currently one clause inside a sentence about rule counts, and that clause is wrong — it describes one of seven shapes as if it were the bar. The bar is the most consequential mechanism in §7.4 (it is what turns detection into a hold on the *next* action) and it deserves the seven shapes listed with their reason slugs, the note that the obfuscation shape needs only one finding, and the note that the monitor lane is held out of it by design.

3. **Give §7.5 the three-surface structure its title promises, and put uninstall under quarantine.** Today MCP gets four paragraphs, plugins two, skills none. Proposed: **MCP** (discovery and its bounds; static risk; the remote handshake; identity), **Plugins** (two gates, four surfaces, the shim gate's fail-open), **Skills** (the two-axis load gate — currently absent entirely), then a shared **Quarantine and restore** subsection covering all three stash systems side by side. That last consolidation is what makes the two errors in the current text impossible to repeat: the "all three refuse on backup digest" claim is only visible as wrong when the three are compared in one place, and the Windows-MSI-only-preserves fact has no home in the current layout at all.

4. **Change §7.6's framing from intent to evidence.** "What we deliberately do not do" is a claim about design decisions, and two of its five bullets are actually claims about code that exists and does not run. Retitle it "What this product does not do, and why" and split each bullet into the choice (never built) and the state (built, not wired). The two are opposite facts about the product and currently read identically. Cross-reference the INERT items in §7.4 rather than restating them, so there is one register of dead code and not two.

One editorial note that applies across all four sections: several numbers here are load-bearing and none of them currently carries the file it came from. `18 rules`, `16 locations`, `5 classes / 17 rules`, `five error paths`, `30 minutes`, `1024` — each of these is one grep from being checkable, and each one that is wrong (`7 classes`, `four checkpoints`) is wrong in a way a citation would have caught at writing time. Recommend a bracketed source path after each count, as §19 already does for the code map.
